title: Audit flags ₹13,678 crore in defective planning across central public sector firms
dek: The CAG's compliance audit for 2024-25 identifies ₹20,539.40 crore in financial implications, with the largest share attributed to planning failures, while the managements' replies remain partly unincorporated.
theme: Defective planning in central public sector enterprises
indiaConnection: This audit examines how a public programme in India was carried out and recorded, and it states what the audited record can and cannot establish for the people in India who depend on it.

eventTime.label: Date not established in the supplied evidence

body.text: For the fiscal year ending 31 March 2025, the Comptroller and Auditor General of India's compliance audit found total financial effects of ₹20,539.40 crore across 15 observations. The biggest share, ₹13,678.68 crore, stems from flawed or insufficient planning as detailed in eight paragraphs. Additionally, the audit highlighted ₹609.70 crore in seven paragraphs for failing to protect organisational financial interests, ₹5,900.81 crore in four paragraphs for weak or insufficient oversight, and ₹350.21 crore in four paragraphs for breaching rules and contract terms.

The audit's breakdown acknowledges that a single paragraph can include issues from several groups, meaning the sums are not exclusive. No breakdown is offered to show how much of the overall total belongs to each group without double-counting. Consequently, these numbers reflect the audit's own grouping rather than a strict separation of distinct concerns.

According to the audit report, preliminary observations were forwarded to the relevant central public sector enterprises, and their feedback was properly integrated. Yet, the report notes four paragraphs where the concerned ministry or department had not yet given its response, with one each from the Coal, Tourism, and Petroleum and Natural Gas sectors, and one from Power. This suggests that some managements had not replied by the time the report was prepared.

section.title: The managements' replies and the audit's response

body.text: The audit does not disclose the content of the managements' replies or how they were incorporated. It only states that the replies were suitably incorporated, without specifying whether they were accepted, rejected, or partially addressed. This leaves the reader unable to assess the validity of the audit's findings against the managements' own accounts.

The audit report includes a chapter on recoveries and corrections made by the CPSEs at the instance of audit. It states that managements of 11 CPSEs recovered an amount of ₹60.02 crore during 2024-25, and that three CPSEs carried out corrections or rectifications in five cases. These actions are presented as a positive outcome of the audit process, but the report does not provide details on the nature of the corrections or the specific cases.

section.title: Recoveries and corrections at the instance of audit

body.text: The audit does not connect these recoveries and corrections to the specific observations in the report. It is unclear whether the recovered amounts relate to the financial implications identified in the audit observations or to other issues. The report also does not state whether the corrections were made in response to the draft observations or were initiated independently.

The audit report covers only the period and sample it names, and it does not provide independent verification of the managements' claims. The report's findings are based on the audit's examination of the CPSEs' records, but it does not include external evidence or testimony from people affected by the issues. This limits the ability to confirm the accuracy of the audit's categorisations or the effectiveness of the corrective actions.

section.title: What the record does not establish

body.text: The report does not specify the timeline for when the audit observations were made or when the managements' replies were received. It also does not provide a breakdown of the financial implications by individual CPSE or by ministry, beyond the aggregate figures. This makes it difficult to assess the distribution of the problems across the public sector.
